_readme: The short list worth reading FIRST per resource type we actually run — judgement the API
cannot supply. `list_metrics` says what EXISTS; this says what MATTERS, and what each
number would mean if it moved.
This catalog is a shortcut, never a limit: anything absent here is still reachable through
list_monitored_resources + list_metrics, which is why it stays short instead of growing a
line per GCP service. Keep it that way — an exhaustive hand-maintained catalog is stale
the week after it is written.
A `metric` here is a best-known type, not a guarantee: Google renames and splits metric
families between service generations. A wrong type is SAFE — read_timeseries resolves the
descriptor first, so an unknown type fails loudly instead of returning a plausible number
for a different question. When one errors, fall back to list_metrics on the prefix.

memorystore_instance.note: The Valkey generation. Classic Memorystore for Redis publishes under redis.googleapis.com — both families can exist in the same project, so read the one your instance answers on. Every metric below was confirmed against the live API.
memorystore_instance.first_question: Is the MAIN THREAD saturated? Valkey is single-threaded, so the node average is the wrong number — it stays low while the one thread that matters is pinned.

metrics.answers: The busiest CPU on the instance — for a single-threaded server, effectively the main thread. THE metric for a Valkey latency question. Aligns ALIGN_MAX automatically.
metrics.watch_for: Above ~70% queueing delay starts to compound even though nothing is 'full': at 80% utilization a caller waits several times the service time, which is how commands that execute in microseconds turn into hundreds of milliseconds at the caller. Measured on a production instance: trough 53.3% mean, daytime 58.6%, traffic peak 71.2% mean / 82.5% max — heavily queued, and still not capped.

metrics.answers: Averaged across CPUs. Useful only as the CONTRAST to maximum_utilization — a wide gap between the two is the signature of a single-threaded workload on a multi-core node.
metrics.watch_for: Quoting this one alone. It reads comfortable while the main thread is not.

metrics.answers: Per-node, per-CPU-state breakdown (several series per node). Use to see WHICH thread is busy rather than how busy the instance is.
metrics.watch_for: Two series tracking each other high while others sit near zero — the main thread plus its pair, everything else idle.

metrics.answers: How close to the writable ceiling, and therefore how near eviction. Pairs with node/memory/utilization.
metrics.watch_for: A climb with no plateau — an unbounded key family, e.g. a consumer group's pending list. Flat means memory is NOT your problem — one instance measured here sat at ~33% across an entire peak while its CPU climbed.

metrics.answers: CPU spent in the expiry cycle. A DELTA counter, so it aligns as a RATE. One of the few in-server stalls that can block a single-threaded event loop without appearing as command time.
metrics.watch_for: A rise tracking the latency window — expiry work stealing the thread the commands need.

redis_instance.note: Can be present alongside the Valkey family in the same project. Names below verified against the live API.
redis_instance.first_question: Same as Valkey: the busiest thread first, then memory.

metrics.answers: Per-node CPU as a GAUGE — the comparable of the Valkey metric above, and the one to reach for first.
The busiest node/CPU in the cluster. ALIGN_MAX.
CPU seconds consumed — a DELTA counter in seconds, NOT a ratio, so it aligns as a RATE and is not comparable to the utilization gauges above. Do not read it as a percentage.
metrics.watch_for: Mistaking this for the utilization metric; the unit is s{CPU}.

metrics.answers: Fraction of the memory ceiling in use, worst node.

cloudsql_database.note: The INSTANCE-level view. Per-statement numbers live on a different monitored resource — see cloudsql_instance_database below; the insights/* metrics cannot be filtered by this type's labels.
cloudsql_database.first_question: Is the instance saturated, or is it the connection pool in front of it?

metrics.answers: Instance CPU. ALIGN_MAX.
Memory pressure — a fall in cache hit rate usually shows here first.
Backends in use. Compare against max_connections before blaming query time.
metrics.watch_for: A ceiling — clients then queue outside the database, which its own spans cannot see.

metrics.answers: Disk headroom; a full disk takes writes down hard.
Transaction rate — the load denominator for every other number here.

cloudsql_instance_database.note: A DIFFERENT monitored resource from cloudsql_database, addressed by DIFFERENT labels — project_id, location, resource_id (formatted 'project:instance') and database. Filtering an insights metric by cloudsql_database's `database_id` fails with HTTP 400 'The supplied filter does not specify a valid combination of metric and monitored resource descriptors', which reads like a bad metric name rather than a wrong resource type — resolve the resource with list_monitored_resources first. These carry data only where Query Insights is ENABLED on the instance; confirmed against the live API on an instance where it is. aggregate/* (per user per database) and pertag/* carry the same six measures at coarser grain.
cloudsql_instance_database.first_question: WHICH statement burned the time? cloudsql_database says the instance was saturated; this says what saturated it.

metrics.answers: Accumulated execution time per normalized statement — CPU plus IO wait, lock wait, context switch and scheduling. CUMULATIVE us{CPU}, so it aligns as a RATE and reads as microseconds of execution per second of wall clock. The metric labels carry `querystring` — the FULL normalized SQL, not merely a hash — with `query_hash` and `user`.
metrics.watch_for: Often the ONLY route to production SQL text: pg_stat_statements is not installed by default on a managed instance, so check pg_extension before assuming the database itself can answer it. Two series can share a querystring under different query_hash values — do not merge them by text.

metrics.answers: Lock wait per statement — what separates 'slow' from 'blocked by someone else'.
Per-statement latency as a DISTRIBUTION, so it aligns to p99 rather than to a mean.
The same total per user per database with no statement breakdown — the denominator to check a per-query reading against.
metrics.watch_for: A per-query sum far below this total means series hit the MAX_SERIES cap. Read `series_dropped` before ranking anything: the kept series are the API's own order (alphabetical by querystring), NOT the largest.

k8s_node.first_question: Is the node out of room, or is the pod simply not being given more?

metrics.answers: How much of the node's allocatable CPU is claimed. ALIGN_MAX.
The same for memory — the number that precedes an eviction.

k8s_container.first_question: Is the container throttled against its own limit? A pod can be slow on an idle node.

metrics.answers: Usage against the container's CPU limit. ALIGN_MAX. Near 1.0 means CFS throttling, which reads as latency, not as an error.
metrics.watch_for: High limit_utilization while the NODE is idle — the fix is the limit, not the node.

metrics.answers: Usage against the memory limit — the run-up to an OOMKill.
Restarts. A counter, so it aligns as a rate: any non-zero rate is a crash loop.

gce_instance.first_question: CPU ceiling, then network — in that order.

metrics.answers: VM CPU. ALIGN_MAX.
Inbound traffic — the load denominator, and a bandwidth ceiling in its own right.

https_lb_rule.first_question: Did the delay happen before our code ever saw the request?

metrics.answers: End-to-end latency at the edge, as a DISTRIBUTION — aligns to p99 automatically. Compare against the service's own span: the difference is time our traces cannot see.
metrics.watch_for: Edge latency far above service latency — the delay is queueing in front of us.

metrics.answers: Backend-only latency. Subtracting this from total isolates the edge's own overhead.
Request rate, groupable by response_code_class — the fastest way to see a 5xx band.
